summary: Defines generic matching rules that can match any attribute in LDAP or X.500 directories, even those with complex structured syntax. Matching rules defined for complex syntaxes usually only offer the most immediately useful matching, and this broadens that. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Looking things up in a directory is easy for simple words but hard for complicated entries. This gives a general way to compare any part of a complicated entry.

questions: how to match parts of complex ldap attributes
how to search inside a complex ldap attribute
subtitle: Generic matching rules that let LDAP and X.500 searches look inside any structured attribute value.

tldr.problem: Directory attributes can have complex structured syntaxes, but their matching rules usually only offer the most immediately useful comparison, and some have no equality rule at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a ComponentAssertion that points at a part of an ASN.1 value and tests it with an existing matching rule, a ComponentFilter that combines assertions with and, or and not, and new rules including componentFilterMatch and allComponentsMatch.
tldr.outcome: Any attribute whose syntax is described by an ASN.1 type can be searched by its parts, without writing a bespoke matching rule for each syntax.

today: RFC 3687 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of these component matching rules.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The data in an LDAP or X.500 directory attribute is described by the attribute's syntax. Syntaxes range from simple types such as text string, integer or boolean to complex ones, for example the syntaxes of the directory schema operational attributes. In X.500 they are given as ASN.1 type definitions; in LDAP they are usually given in ABNF, with an implied link to the ASN.1 type.

With a complex syntax you often want to match only some components of a value. Matching rules written for one syntax usually offer only the most immediately useful matching, and some complex syntaxes have no equality matching rule at all. RFC 3687 instead defines a generic way to match user-selected components of an attribute value of any syntax described in ASN.1 notation.

The RFC also notes that syntaxes defined only by a character string encoding, with no explicit or implied ASN.1 type, cannot use these rules until a semantically equivalent ASN.1 type is defined for them.
sections.eli5: Some directory entries are like a form with many boxes. Until now, a search could usually only check the most popular box. This lets a search check any box you pick.

sections.title: The ComponentAssertion
sections.content:
A ComponentAssertion is a testable statement about the presence or values of components inside an ASN.1 value, normally an attribute value. It evaluates to TRUE, FALSE or Undefined. It has four fields:

  • component: which part to test (OPTIONAL; if absent, the whole value is tested).
  • useDefaultValues: whether DEFAULT values stand in for absent components (default TRUE).
  • rule: the matching rule used for the test, given as an object identifier.
  • value: the asserted value to compare against; its type is set by the chosen rule.

The assertion is TRUE if at least one identified component value makes the matching rule return TRUE, and FALSE otherwise, including when no component values exist. It is Undefined if, among other cases, the rule is unknown, does not apply to the component type, the asserted value does not fit the rule's assertion syntax, or an open type cannot be decoded.
sections.eli5: An assertion is one yes-or-no question about one part of an entry, such as "does this box say foobar?". The answer can also be "cannot tell" if the question does not make sense for that box.

sections.title: Component References
sections.content:
The component field holds a component reference, a UTF-8 string of one or more ComponentIds separated by dots. Each one steps one level deeper into the value. A reference may point at a complex component as well as a simple one.

For SET, SEQUENCE and CHOICE types, an identifier names a component or alternative. For SET OF and SEQUENCE OF types the RFC offers a number counting from the beginning (starting at one), a negative number counting from the end (-1 is the last), 0 for the notional count of instances, and an asterisk for all instances at once. The asterisk form is the way one reference can identify several values. A parenthesised select form picks one permitted type inside an ASN.1 open type, and content reaches contained types.

Wrappers that do not matter for matching, such as type references, tags and constraints, are stripped away automatically before each step.

The RFC's example type has a SET OF OBJECT IDENTIFIER named part3. There part3.2 is the second instance, part3.0 is the count and part3.* is every instance.
sections.eli5: A component reference is like directions inside a building: second floor, third door, top shelf. Each dot takes you one step deeper to the exact thing you want to check.

sections.title: Matching Components and Two New Rules
sections.content:
Existing attribute matching rules do the actual testing, applied to the referenced component. If the component's type is a tagged or constrained form of the type a rule expects, further substitutions reduce it to the expected type. The existing case ignore and case exact string rules are extended, for component matching only, to the restricted character string types and to any ChoiceOfStrings type. The telephone number rules may be applied to any PrintableString, and distinguishedNameMatch to RDNSequence values.

Two new rules are defined. rdnMatch tests one Relative Distinguished Name inside a DN without regard to the other RDNs. Because the LDAP encoding of a DN reverses the order of the RDNs, the RDN cn=Steven Legg in cn=Steven Legg,o=Adacel,c=AU is component reference 3, or alternatively -1. presentMatch tests only whether a component is present, whatever its contents; in a ComponentAssertion it is TRUE if and only if the reference identifies one or more component values.

An absent SET OF value is different from a present but empty one. If a SET OF is present but empty, presentMatch on it returns TRUE and the notional count is present and equal to zero.
sections.eli5: The old question-askers like "is this the same word?" still do the checking. This part just teaches them to look at a single piece, and adds two new askers: "is this the same address label?" and "is anything written here at all?"

sections.title: ComponentFilter and componentFilterMatch
sections.content:
One assertion tests one component. A ComponentFilter combines assertions. It is a CHOICE of item (a single ComponentAssertion), and, or (each a list of filters) and not (one filter). The order of filters inside and and or is not significant.

Evaluation follows three-valued logic. An and is TRUE if the list is empty or every filter is TRUE, FALSE if at least one is FALSE, and Undefined otherwise. An or is FALSE if the list is empty or every filter is FALSE, TRUE if at least one is TRUE, and Undefined otherwise. A not flips TRUE and FALSE and leaves Undefined as it is.

The componentFilterMatch matching rule applies a ComponentFilter to an attribute value. Its assertion value is encoded using the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER), with prefixes such as item:, and:, or: and not:. Because a ComponentAssertion can use any rule, componentFilterMatch can be nested, and references in the inner filter are relative to the component picked by the outer assertion.
sections.eli5: Questions can be joined with "and", "or" and "not", like "has a pet and does not have a cat". This section is the rulebook for joining the questions and for what to do when one cannot be answered.

sections.title: Equality Matching of Whole Values
sections.content:
Instead of a long filter checking every part, allComponentsMatch compares a whole assertion value against an attribute or component value part by part. It is TRUE if and only if corresponding components are the same, applied recursively. For example, two SEQUENCE values match when each component is both absent, both present and the same, or absent or equal to the DEFAULT. Two SET OF values match when they have the same instances, including duplicates, in any order. String comparison is case sensitive, and tags and constraints are ignored. If the actual type of an open type value is unknown, the result is Undefined.

Refined rules can be derived from it with a table naming, for chosen types or components, a commutative equality rule that overrides the default. Rows for an outer type take precedence over rows for an inner type, and earlier rows win over later ones. The RFC defines directoryComponentsMatch this way: it uses distinguishedNameMatch for RDNSequence, rdnMatch for a stand-alone RelativeDistinguishedName, telephoneNumberMatch for telephone numbers, numericStringMatch, generalizedTimeMatch and uTCTimeMatch for those types, and caseIgnoreMatch for the other string types. Both rules may be the defined equality rule for an attribute.
sections.eli5: allComponentsMatch is a careful "are these two forms exactly alike?" check that compares every box. directoryComponentsMatch is the same check, but it ignores capital letters in words, which is what people usually want.

sections.title: Worked Search Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's examples search the objectClasses schema attribute, whose syntax is ObjectClassDescription, a SEQUENCE with fields such as identifier, name (a SET OF strings), description (OPTIONAL) and obsolete.

  • Matching identifier with objectIdentifierMatch finds the class with OID 2.5.6.18. This subsumes objectIdentifierFirstComponentMatch, integerFirstComponentMatch and directoryStringFirstComponentMatch.
  • Matching name.* with caseIgnoreMatch finds a class called foobar, even if it has several names.
  • Matching name.0 with integerMatch and value 1 finds classes with exactly one name.
  • presentMatch on description finds classes that have a description, and wrapping it in not: finds those without one.
sections.eli5: Here are real questions you could ask a directory: "find the class with this number", "find the class with this name", "find classes that have a description". Each one is a short recipe using the pieces from earlier.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the component matching rules behave like any other matching rule, so their security issues are no different. There is one added point: because the rules apply to any attribute syntax, a directory server that supports them may allow searching of attributes that were previously unsearchable for lack of a suitable matching rule. Such attributes ought to be properly protected with appropriate access controls.

The RFC adds that a generic, interoperable access control mechanism has not yet been developed, and implementors should be aware of how that lack interacts with the increased exposure.
sections.eli5: Being able to search more places also means people could peek at things that used to be hard to search. So private entries need good locks.
